narrative:
The model determined that you have a 90% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process heavily weighs this predicted outcome, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your performance in your third year of law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. This was followed by your LSAT score, which also pulled the outcome heavily in the same negative direction. Your first-year performance ranked third and further increased the likelihood of failure.

In each case, your results fell well below those of students who were accepted. Your first-year and third-year class rankings placed you in the bottom decile, compared to an average around the middle of the class for accepted students. Your LSAT score of 19.3 was also substantially lower than the average of 37.2 among those who received offers. These academic signals were so consistent and below benchmark that the model concluded a first-time bar passage was highly unlikely.

Your family income and plan to attend full-time had little effect on the outcome. Gender and race played no role whatsoever in the prediction.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Once those indicators move closer to the levels seen in successful applicants, the model would likely view your prospects for passing the bar much more favorably. (218 words)
